title: The Difference Between Uptime and a Healthy Product
content:
A website can return a successful response while its users cannot complete their task. The homepage may load even though checkout fails; the API may answer quickly with stale data; a login page may be reachable while authentication is broken. Uptime measures a useful slice of availability, but product health asks whether the important journeys still work for the people who depend on them. Operational checks should connect infrastructure signals to user outcomes.

Define the user journey first

List a small set of critical journeys: sign in, find an item, submit a form, complete a purchase, or retrieve an account record. For each, state the result a user expects and the dependencies involved. A synthetic request to the root URL may confirm that a server answers; it does not prove those journeys. Conversely, a single failed synthetic request may reflect a monitoring problem rather than broad customer impact. Define both the probe and its interpretation.

The Google SRE chapter on service level objectives distinguishes a service level indicator from an objective and advises choosing measurements that reflect what users care about. The indicator needs a precise population: which requests, regions, users, and time window count? A success percentage that excludes timeouts or counts only the easiest endpoint can make a service appear healthy while a crucial path is failing.

Separate availability from correctness

Basic uptime checks answer whether a designated endpoint responds. Add checks for valid content and essential side effects. A search endpoint may return HTTP 200 and an empty result set because its index is stale. A confirmation page may appear although an order was never stored. Validate the response shape, freshness, and state change where the journey requires them. Avoid invasive probes that create real charges or send messages to customers; use controlled test accounts and cleanup rules.

Watch for partial failure. A CDN can serve cached public pages while the origin API is unavailable. One region may work while another fails. A mobile client may be broken by a response shape that desktop code tolerates. Segment metrics by the dimensions that help locate a problem, but do not create so many slices that every tiny sample becomes an alert. Pair a broad view of user impact with enough detail for diagnosis.

Use more than one operational signal

The Google SRE monitoring chapter presents latency, traffic, errors, and saturation as four useful signals for user-facing systems. A rising error rate is obvious, but a sudden drop in traffic may indicate clients cannot reach the service. Latency can rise before errors do. Saturation can warn that the system is running out of capacity. These signals help explain a failure; they do not by themselves tell you whether a particular user task completed.

Instrument the key journey where possible. A checkout completion ratio, message-delivery confirmation, or successful document retrieval can complement server metrics. Define the denominator carefully. A ratio of completed checkouts to page views may change because of marketing traffic or user intent, not software failure. Operational alerts should favor a metric close to a technical failure and be reviewed against a product-level signal before sweeping conclusions.

Choose an objective and response

An SLO can state the intended reliability level over a defined period. Set it from user needs and business consequences, then use error budget or breach patterns to guide release pace and repair work. Avoid a universal promise of 100 percent availability. A target that is too loose can conceal harm; one that is needlessly strict can redirect effort away from other valuable work. State what happens when the objective is missed: who investigates, which changes pause, and what evidence confirms recovery.

Document incident severity using user impact, not just machine alarms. An unavailable internal dashboard for a small group may be less urgent than a working homepage with broken password reset for everyone. Define escalation and ownership before the incident. A healthy product includes support and communication paths: users need a clear status and an alternative route when a critical feature fails.

A hypothetical booking service

Imagine a hypothetical booking site whose load balancer reports continuous uptime. Its calendar endpoint responds 200, but a new data-cache rule serves availability from yesterday. Visitors see slots, submit a booking, and receive a rejection. A heartbeat probe remains green. The team adds a controlled journey check that selects a synthetic slot, validates the availability timestamp, and stops before a real charge. It also tracks booking submission failures by cause.

During a later cache problem, the freshness check fails while the root URL still loads. Engineers bypass the stale cache, verify that a fresh slot can be held, and then inspect affected booking attempts. This is a hypothetical example, not a claim of a measured incident. Its lesson is that availability and correctness require different evidence and recovery steps.

Review the monitoring system

After an incident, ask whether an alert arrived before users reported trouble, whether it described impact accurately, and whether responders had enough context. Remove noisy alerts that trigger without action, and add checks for blind spots revealed by real failures. A monitoring dashboard is a maintained product. If nobody owns a signal or knows what to do when it changes, the signal is unlikely to protect users.

Product-health checklist

  • Name critical journeys and expected outcomes.
  • Define uptime probes and their limits.
  • Check correctness, freshness, and side effects where relevant.
  • Track latency, traffic, errors, and saturation.
  • Use precise populations and windows for indicators.
  • Set response ownership and user-impact thresholds.
  • Verify recovery through the journey that failed.
  • Revisit checks after incidents and product changes.
excerpt: Uptime shows whether an endpoint responds; product health checks whether critical user journeys complete correctly, promptly, and with fresh data.
